course_description: Examines African American history from 1865 to the present. Emphasizes regional, gender, and class distinction within African American communities, and the ways in which industrial transformations shaped African American life, thought, and resistance.
course_notes: (Same as HIST 239 1) (Following the end of the Civil War in 1865, African Americans confronted a nation that promised citizenship and equality while simultaneously creating new systems of racial control, segregation, and disenfranchisement. In the face of inequality, African Americans continuously challenged injustice, established intellectual and social communities, and maintained hope for the future. This drive reshaped American culture while contributing to the true American definition of what freedom and citizenship entailed. We will examine African American history following the Civil War and Reconstruction through the modern day. As we trace through time, we will examine the rise of Jim Crow, the Great Migration, the Harlem Renaissance, two World Wars, the Cold War, and the Civil Rights and Black Power Movements, among other points of political and social struggles throughout the late nineteenth and twentieth centuries. By centering the experiences and contributions of African Americans, we will explore how equality and identity have been constructed over the last century and a half. We will also assess the impact of gender, class, and colonialism had in shaping African American experiences. Through readings, discussion, and multimedia sources, we will reimagine African American history as a summation of ongoing struggles over power, justice, and inclusion.)
